claim: The synchronization of canonical fast sleep spindle activity (12.5–16 Hz, adult-like) precisely during the slow oscillation (0.5–1 Hz) up peak is considered an essential feature of adult non-rapid eye movement sleep.
source: The synchronization of canonical fast sleep spindle activity (12.5–16 Hz, adult-like) precisely during the slow oscillation (0.5–1 Hz) up peak is considered an essential feature of adult non-rapid eye movement sleep.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about adult NREM sleep characteristics.

claim: The predominant type of fast spindles was development-specific in that it was still nested in a frequency range below the canonical fast spindle range for the majority of children.
source: While the predominant type of fast spindles was development-specific in that it was still nested in a frequency range below the canonical fast spindle range for the majority of children, the well-known slow oscillation-spindle coupling pattern was evident for sleep spindles in the adult-like canonical fast spindle range in all four age groups—but notably less precise in children.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1A-B showing that for most young children, the peak frequencies and frequencies of dominant fast spindles were slower than the canonical fast sleep spindle band.

claim: The slow oscillation-spindle coupling pattern was evident for sleep spindles in the adult-like canonical fast spindle range in all four age groups.
source: While the predominant type of fast spindles was development-specific in that it was still nested in a frequency range below the canonical fast spindle range for the majority of children, the well-known slow oscillation-spindle coupling pattern was evident for sleep spindles in the adult-like canonical fast spindle range in all four age groups—but notably less precise in children.
evidence: This is supported by the PETH analyses shown in Figure 4B demonstrating coupling patterns across all age groups.

claim: Slow oscillation-spindle coupling was notably less precise in children compared to older age groups.
source: While the predominant type of fast spindles was development-specific in that it was still nested in a frequency range below the canonical fast spindle range for the majority of children, the well-known slow oscillation-spindle coupling pattern was evident for sleep spindles in the adult-like canonical fast spindle range in all four age groups—but notably less precise in children.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal precision analyses shown in Figure 4 and the PETH results.

claim: Fast spindle maturity was uniquely associated with enhanced slow oscillation-spindle coupling strength across the four age groups.
source: Importantly, we found that fast spindle maturity was uniquely associated with enhanced slow oscillation-spindle coupling strength and temporal precision across the four age groups.
evidence: This is supported by the GLMM analysis showing that higher fast spindle maturity was associated with stronger modulation of development-specific fast centro-parietal sleep spindles during SOs (β = 0.50, t = 8.97, p < 0.001).

claim: Fast spindle maturity was uniquely associated with enhanced slow oscillation-spindle coupling temporal precision across the four age groups.
source: Importantly, we found that fast spindle maturity was uniquely associated with enhanced slow oscillation-spindle coupling strength and temporal precision across the four age groups.
evidence: This is supported by the PLSC analysis showing that fast spindle maturity was associated with more adult-like SO-spindle coupling patterns (Figure 6A-B).

claim: The increasing ability to generate adult-like canonical fast sleep spindles actuates precise slow oscillation-spindle coupling patterns from childhood through adolescence and into young adulthood.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the increasing ability to generate adult-like canonical fast sleep spindles actuates precise slow oscillation-spindle coupling patterns from childhood through adolescence and into young adulthood.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined findings from spindle maturity analyses and coupling strength measurements.

claim: The grouping of sleep spindles (9–16 Hz) into sequences of increased and decreased activity by the sleep slow oscillation (SO, 0.5–1 Hz) during non-rapid eye movement sleep has been recognized as an intrinsic property of the healthy, mature mammalian corticothalamic system for decades.
source: The grouping of sleep spindles (9–16 Hz; Cox et al., 2017) into sequences of increased and decreased activity by the sleep slow oscillation (SO, 0.5–1 Hz; Steriade, 2006) during non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREM) has been recognized as an intrinsic property of the healthy, mature mammalian corticothalamic system for decades (Contreras et al., 1996; Contreras and Steriade, 1995; Mulle et al., 1986; Staresina et al., 2015; Steriade et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The joint depolarization of large groups of cortical neurons during the SO up state impinges on neurons of the reticular thalamic nucleus, creating conditions that facilitate thalamic spindle generation.
source: The joint depolarization of large groups of cortical neurons during the SO up state impinges on neurons of the reticular thalamic nucleus, there, creating conditions that facilitate thalamic spindle generation (Steriade, 1999).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Steriade, 1999.

claim: Sleep spindles propagate to the cortex via thalamocortical projections, where they promote synaptic plasticity through changes in calcium activity.
source: Sleep spindles then propagate to the cortex via thalamocortical projections, where they promote synaptic plasticity through changes in calcium activity (Niethard et al., 2018; Rosanova and Ulrich, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Niethard et al., 2018 and Rosanova and Ulrich, 2005.

claim: The synchronization of canonical fast sleep spindles precisely during the up state of SOs provides an essential mechanism for neural communication, supporting systems memory consolidation during sleep.
source: Far from being an epiphenomenon, accumulating evidence suggests that the synchronization of canonical fast sleep spindles (i.e., spindles defined in young adults with a frequency of ≈ 12.5–16 Hz and a centro-parietal predominance; Cox et al., 2017) precisely during the up state of SOs provides an essential mechanism for neural communication, for example, supporting systems memory consolidation during sleep (Hahn et al., 2020; Helfrich et al., 2018; Latchoumane et al., 2017; Mölle et al., 2002; Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on memory consolidation.

claim: Canonical fast spindles assort hippocampal ripples that code for wake experiences and are considered a reliable marker of hippocampal memory consolidation.
source: Importantly, canonical fast spindles in turn assort hippocampal ripples (Clemens et al., 2007; Helfrich et al., 2019; Siapas and Wilson, 1998; Staresina et al., 2015), that code for wake experiences and are considered a reliable marker of hippocampal memory consolidation (Buzsáki, 2015; Maingret et al., 2016; Sirota et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Canonical fast sleep spindles are associated with facilitated hippocampal-neocortical connectivity.
source: Moreover, canonical fast sleep spindles themselves are associated with facilitated hippocampal-neocortical connectivity (Andrade et al., 2011; Cowan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andrade et al., 2011 and Cowan et al., 2020.

claim: There is substantial evidence for a canonical slow sleep spindle type with a frequency of ≈ 9–12.5 Hz and a frontal predominance in the human surface electroencephalogram.
source: In addition to canonical fast sleep spindles, there is substantial evidence for a canonical slow sleep spindle type (i.e., spindles defined in young adults with a frequency of ≈ 9–12.5 Hz and a frontal predominance; Cox et al., 2017) in the human surface electroencephalogram (EEG; De Gennaro and Ferrara, 2003; Fernandez and Lüthi, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous findings hint at a differential SO-slow spindle coupling pattern and their function is still elusive.
source: That said, previous findings hint at a differential SO-slow spindle coupling pattern and their function is still elusive (Klinzing et al., 2016; Mölle et al., 2011; Muehlroth et al., 2019; Rasch and Born, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research indicating uncertainty about slow spindle function.

claim: The complex wave sequence of SO up state and canonical fast sleep spindles, together with hippocampal activity, is considered to provide the scaffold for the precisely timed reactivation of initially fragile hippocampal memory representations and their strengthening in neocortical networks.
source: Taken together, the complex wave sequence of SO up state and canonical fast sleep spindles, together with hippocampal activity, is considered to provide the scaffold for the precisely timed reactivation of initially fragile hippocampal memory representations and their strengthening in neocortical networks (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Helfrich et al., 2019; Maingret et al., 2016; Staresina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on memory consolidation mechanisms.

claim: The precise coupling of sleep spindle activity to SOs does not seem to be fully present and functional from early childhood on.
source: However, the precise coupling of sleep spindle activity to SOs, described above, does not seem to be fully present and functional from early childhood on.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citation to recent evidence in rodents and humans.

claim: The temporal co-ordination of SOs and spindles improves across childhood and adolescence.
source: Recent evidence in rodents and humans indicates that the temporal co-ordination of SOs and spindles improves across childhood and adolescence (García-Pérez et al., 2022; Hahn et al., 2020; Joechner et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research in both rodents and humans.

claim: Sleep spindles increase in occurrence across maturation.
source: Across maturation, sleep spindles increase in occurrence and their average frequency (Purcell et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Purcell et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Sleep spindles increase in their average frequency across maturation.
source: Across maturation, sleep spindles increase in occurrence and their average frequency (Purcell et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Purcell et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Canonical slow sleep spindles mature and dominate during early childhood.
source: Consistent with this, canonical slow sleep spindles were reported to mature and dominate during early childhood.
evidence: This is stated as consistent with previous findings about spindle development.

claim: Canonical fast spindles are rarely detected in young children and become increasingly present and clearly dissociable only around puberty.
source: In contrast, canonical fast spindles are rarely detected in young children and become increasingly present and clearly dissociable only around puberty (D'Atri et al., 2018; Goldstone et al., 2019; Hoedlmoser et al., 2014; Shinomiya et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous developmental research.

claim: Young children express functional fast spindles in centro-parietal sites in a development-specific fashion.
source: However, amongst others, the application of individually adjusted frequency bands revealed that already young children express functional fast spindles in centro-parietal sites, whereby these manifest in a development-specific fashion (D'Atri et al., 2018; Friedrich et al., 2019; Joechner et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using individualized frequency band approaches.

claim: Individualized rhythm detection methods provide an effective approach to capture true, dominant oscillatory rhythms despite substantial inter-individual variability.
source: Individualized rhythm detection methods provide an effective approach to capture true, dominant oscillatory rhythms despite substantial inter-individual variability, which presents a particular methodological challenge in developmental and age-comparative research (Cox et al., 2017; Muehlroth and Werkle-Bergner, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Slow oscillations show an opposite trend to canonical fast spindles across development, with maximal expression initially that decreases with age.
source: While canonical fast spindles become more pronounced across development, an opposite trend can be observed for SOs (Buchmann et al., 2011; Kurth et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buchmann et al., 2011 and Kurth et al., 2010a.

claim: Slow neuronal activity initially originates over posterior areas and develops towards a mature anterior predominance.
source: Slow neuronal activity is initially maximally expressed and originates over posterior areas, developing towards a mature anterior predominance (Kurth et al., 2010b; Timofeev et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurth et al., 2010b and Timofeev et al., 2020.

claim: The study analyzed 24 5- to 6-year-old children (13 female, mean age = 5 years, 10.71 months, SD = 7.28 months).
source: Therefore, we aimed to (i) characterize the modulation of sleep spindles during SOs across different ages and (ii) investigate how sleep spindle and SO maturity relate to the manifestation of SO-spindle coupling across different ages. Specifically, based on previous analyses (Joechner et al., 2021), we reasoned that the development of fast sleep spindles might be associated with the maturation of SO-spindle coupling. For this, we re-analyzed previously published nocturnal EEG data from a cross-sectional sample of 24 5- to 6-year-old children (13 female, Mage = 5 years, 10.71 months, SDage = 7.28 months; Joechner et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The study analyzed a longitudinal cohort of 33 children tested at 8–11 years of age (T1) and again at 14–18 years of age (T2).
source: and a longitudinal cohort of 33 children tested at 8–11 years of age (T1; Hoedlmoser et al., 2014) and again at 14–18 years of age (T2; 23 female, MageT1 = 9 years, 11.70 months, SDageT1 = 8.35 months; MageT2 = 16 years, 4.91 months, SDageT2 = 9.06 months; Hahn et al., 2019; Hahn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the longitudinal study sample.

claim: The study examined a cross-sectional sample of 18 adults aged 20–26 years (15 female, mean age = 21 years, 8.78 months, SD = 20.04 months) as a reference sample for adult-like patterns.
source: Further, we examined a cross-sectional sample of 18 adults aged 20–26 years (15 female, Mage = 21 years, 8.78 months, SDage = 20.04 months) as a reference sample for adult-like patterns.
evidence: This is a description of the adult reference sample.

claim: All cohorts underwent two nights of ambulatory polysomnography.
source: All cohorts underwent two nights of ambulatory polysomnography (PSG).
evidence: This describes the study protocol.

claim: Sleep spindles, SOs, and their coupling were only analyzed during the second night due to well-known first night effects in children.
source: Given well-known first night effects in children (Scholle et al., 2003), sleep spindles, SOs, and their coupling were only analyzed during the second night here.
evidence: This describes the methodological decision based on known first night effects, supported by citation.

claim: Individually identified frontal spindles revealed lower frequencies than centro-parietal sleep spindles across all age groups, indicating the presence of two distinguishably fast spindle types.
source: Hence, across all age groups, individually identified frontal spindles revealed lower frequencies than centro-parietal sleep spindles, indicating the presence of two distinguishably fast spindle types (note, the same applied to the peak frequencies, see Supplementary file 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses showing significant frequency differences between frontal and centro-parietal spindles (all t ≤ –5.38, all padj < 0.001).

claim: For the vast majority of 14- to 18- and 20- to 26-year-olds, individually identified, dominant centro-parietal sleep spindles matched the canonical fast sleep spindle frequency range (≈ 12.5–16 Hz).
source: For the vast majority of 14- to 18- and 20- to 26-year-olds, individually identified, dominant centro-parietal sleep spindles indeed matched the canonical fast sleep spindle frequency range (≈ 12.5–16 Hz, see Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: For the majority of children, dominant fast centro-parietal spindles were nested in the canonical slow spindle range (≈ 9–12.5 Hz) and thus manifested in a development-specific fashion.
source: For the majority of children though, dominant fast centro-parietal spindles were nested in the canonical slow spindle range (i.e., as on average observed in adults with a frequency of ≈ 9–12.5 Hz; Cox et al., 2017) and thus manifested in a development-specific fashion.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Density of slow frontal spindles was higher compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles for the 5- to 6-year-olds (t(136.76) = 5.69, padj < 0.001).
source: For density (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1f), pairwise comparisons indicated higher density for slow frontal compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles for the 5- to 6- (t(136.76) = 5.69, padj < 0.001) and the 8- to 11-year-olds (t(136.76) = 4.62, padj < 0.001)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: Density of slow frontal spindles was higher compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles for the 8- to 11-year-olds (t(136.76) = 4.62, padj < 0.001).
source: For density (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1f), pairwise comparisons indicated higher density for slow frontal compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles for the 5- to 6- (t(136.76) = 5.69, padj < 0.001) and the 8- to 11-year-olds (t(136.76) = 4.62, padj < 0.001)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: Amplitudes were significantly higher for slow frontal as compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles within all age groups (all t ≥ 4.74, all padj ≤ 0.001).
source: For spindle amplitude (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1h), amplitudes were significantly higher for slow frontal as compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles within all age groups (all t ≥ 4.74, all padj ≤ 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: The frequency of adult-like fast sleep spindles was consistently higher as compared to the development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles within all age groups, except the 20- to 26-year-olds.
source: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed that the frequency of adult-like fast sleep spindles was consistently higher as compared to the development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles within all age groups, except the 20- to 26-year-olds (t5-6(135.85) = 18.70, padj 5-6 < 0.001; t8-11(135.85) = 12.48, padj 8-11 < 0.001; t14-18(135.85) = 5.37, padj 14-18 < 0.001; t20-26(135.85) = 2.73, padj 20-26 = 0.199).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: In 5- to 6- and 8- to 11-year-olds, adult-like fast spindles had a lower amplitude compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: In line with a generally higher frequency, in 5- to 6- and 8- to 11-year-olds, adult-like fast spindles had a lower amplitude compared to development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles (t5-6(142.56) = –4.34, padj 5-6 < 0.001; t8-11(142.56) = –4.47, padj 8-11 < 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: The density of development-specific fast sleep spindles was higher compared to adult-like fast spindle density in the 5- to 6- and the 8- to 11-year-olds.
source: Similarly, whereas the density of development-specific fast sleep spindles was higher compared to adult-like fast spindle density in the 5- to 6- and the 8- to 11-year-olds (t5-6(138.60) = –7.66, padj 5-6 < 0.001; t8-11(138.60) = –9.69, padj 8-11 < 0.001), there was no difference in density for the 14- to 18- and 20- to 26-year-olds (t14-18(138.60) = –1.50, padj 14-18 = 1.000; t20-26(138.60) = –0.13, padj 20-26 = 1.000).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: Already young children express adult-like fast spindles which occur increasingly often with older age.
source: Crucially, this indicates that despite the absence of a prominent peak in the power spectrum (Figure 1A), already young children express adult-like fast spindles which occur increasingly often with older age.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the density data showing increasing adult-like fast spindles with age.

claim: Fast centro-parietal spindles become more numerous and adult-like in their frequency and amplitude characteristics in the course of maturation.
source: Hence, fast centro-parietal spindles become more numerous and adult-like in their frequency and amplitude characteristics in the course of maturation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the developmental trends observed in the data.

claim: All age groups, except the 5- to 6-year-olds, expressed SOs at a higher amplitude at frontal as compared to both centro-parietal and occipital locations (all t ≥ 6.68, all p < 0.001).
source: For SO amplitude, inspection of the summary statistics and the pairwise comparisons revealed that all age groups, except the 5- to 6-year-olds, expressed SOs at a higher amplitude at frontal as compared to both centro-parietal and occipital locations (all t ≥ 6.68, all p < 0.001; see Supplementary file 1s and t for all results; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical test results.

claim: A frontal prevalence of SOs was not observed in the youngest children.
source: To summarize, we did not observe a frontal prevalence of SOs in the youngest children.
evidence: This is based on the amplitude analysis showing no frontal dominance in 5-6 year olds.

claim: Frontal dominance of SOs was present in all older age groups (8-11, 14-18, and 20-26 year-olds).
source: However, this dominance was present in all older age groups.
evidence: This is based on the amplitude analysis showing frontal dominance in older age groups.

claim: Within all age groups, power in a broad range including the sleep spindle frequency band (9–16 Hz) was significantly higher during SOs as compared to trials without SOs (all cluster p < 0.001).
source: Within all age groups, power in a broad range including the sleep spindle frequency band (9–16 Hz) was significantly higher during SOs as compared to trials without SOs (all cluster p < 0.001), suggesting temporal clustering of spindles during the SO cycle (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results.

claim: The strongest power differences during SOs as compared to trials without SOs for all four age groups were located within the frequency range of adult-like fast sleep spindles (12.5–16 Hz) within one second after the down peak, close to the up peak.
source: On a descriptive level, the strongest power differences during SOs as compared to trials without SOs for all four age groups were located within the frequency range of adult-like fast sleep spindles (12.5–16 Hz) within one second after the down peak, close to the up peak (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the time-frequency analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: For the 5- to 6-year-olds, there was one positive cluster (p = 0.001) from –700 to –400 ms for the modulation of development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: Statistically, we found one positive cluster (p = 0.001) for the 5- to 6-year-olds from –700 to –400 ms for the modulation of development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles (SO up peak at ≈ 465 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For the 8- to 11-year-olds, there was a positive cluster from –1200 to –400 (p < 0.001) and one negative cluster from –300 to 400 ms (p < 0.001) for development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: For the 8- to 11-year-olds, we identified a more extended positive cluster from –1200 to –400 (p < 0.001) and one negative cluster from –300 to 400 ms (p < 0.001) for development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles (SO up peak at ≈ 488 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For the 14- to 18-year-olds, the analyses indicated two positive clusters (300 to 800 ms, p = 0.002; –1000 to –600 ms, p = 0.014) and two negative clusters (–600 to 200 ms, p < 0.001; 1000 to 1200 ms, p = 0.034) for development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: For the 14- to 18-year-olds, the analyses indicated two positive clusters. One from 300 to 800 ms (p = 0.002) and another from –1000 to –600 ms (p = 0.014) and two negative clusters from –600 to 200 ms (p < 0.001) and from 1000 to 1200 ms (p = 0.034) for development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles (SO up peak at ≈ 532 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For the 20- to 26-year-olds, there was one significant positive cluster (p = 0.005) from 300 to 700 ms and two negative clusters (–500 to 200 ms, p < 0.001; 900 to 1200 ms, p = 0.004) for development-specific fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: For the 20- to 26-year-olds, there was one significant positive cluster (p = 0.005) from 300 to 700 ms and two negative clusters; one from –500 to 200 ms (p < 0.001) and from 900 to 1200 ms (p = 0.004; SO up peak at ≈ 559 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For 5- to 6-year-olds, there was one positive cluster (p < 0.001) from 100 to 500 ms and two negative clusters (both p < 0.001) from –500 to 0 ms and from 700 to 1200 ms for adult-like fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: For 5- to 6-year-olds, we identified one positive cluster (p < 0.001) from 100 to 500 ms and two negative clusters (both p < 0.001) from –500 to 0 ms and from 700 to 1200 ms for adult-like fast centro-parietal spindles (SO up peak at ≈ 465 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For the 8- to 11-year-olds, there were two positive clusters from –1000 to –600 ms (p < 0.001) and from 200 to 600 ms (p = 0.001) and two negative clusters (both p < 0.001) from –400 to 100 ms and from 800 to 1200 ms for adult-like fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: For the 8- to 11-year-olds, we found two positive clusters from –1000 to –600 ms (p < 0.001) and from 200 to 600 ms (p = 0.001) and two negative clusters (both p < 0.001) from –400 to 100 ms and from 800 to 1200 ms (SO up peak at ≈ 488 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For the 14- to 18-year-olds, there was one positive cluster (p < 0.001) from 200 to 800 ms and two negative clusters from –600 to 200 ms (p < 0.001) and from 900 to 1200 ms (p = 0.004) for adult-like fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: For the 14- to 18-year-olds, we identified one positive cluster (p < 0.001) from 200 to 800 ms and two negative clusters from –600 to 200 ms (p < 0.001) and from 900 to 1200 ms (p = 0.004) for adult-like fast centro-parietal spindles (SO up peak at ≈ 532 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: For the 20- to 26-year-olds, analyses revealed one positive cluster (p = 0.003) from 200 to 700 ms and two negative clusters (–500 to 200 ms, p < 0.001; 900 to 1200 ms, p = 0.004) for adult-like fast centro-parietal spindles.
source: Lastly, for the 20- to 26-year-olds, analyses revealed one positive cluster (p = 0.003) from 200 to 700 ms and two negative clusters. One cluster (p < 0.001) from –500 to 200 ms and another one (p = 0.004) from 900 to 1200 ms (SO up peak at ≈ 559 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of cluster-based permutation test results for PETH analysis.

claim: Adult-like fast sleep spindles were already modulated by SOs in the younger age groups—even though they only occurred very rarely.
source: Importantly, adult-like fast sleep spindles were already modulated by SOs in the younger age groups—even though they only occurred very rarely.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the PETH results showing coupling patterns for adult-like fast spindles even in young children.

claim: Independent of the sleep spindle type, increased sleep spindle occurrence was more precisely timed with the SO up peak at older ages.
source: However, independent of the sleep spindle type, increased sleep spindle occurrence was more precisely timed with the SO up peak at older ages.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the PETH patterns across age groups.

claim: Higher fast spindle maturity was associated with stronger modulation of development-specific fast centro-parietal sleep spindles during SOs (β = 0.50, t = 8.97, p < 0.001).
source: The GLMM revealed that only higher fast spindle maturity was associated with stronger modulation of development-specific fast centro-parietal sleep spindles during SOs (β = 0.50, t = 8.97, p < 0.001; see Figure 6C), while SO maturity was not significantly related to the modulation strength (β = 0.09, t = 1.28, p = 0.202).
evidence: This is a direct report of GLMM results.

claim: SO maturity was not significantly related to the modulation strength of development-specific fast centro-parietal sleep spindles during SOs (β = 0.09, t = 1.28, p = 0.202).
source: The GLMM revealed that only higher fast spindle maturity was associated with stronger modulation of development-specific fast centro-parietal sleep spindles during SOs (β = 0.50, t = 8.97, p < 0.001; see Figure 6C), while SO maturity was not significantly related to the modulation strength (β = 0.09, t = 1.28, p = 0.202).
evidence: This is a direct report of GLMM results.

claim: Developmental age differences in the manifestation of SO-spindle coupling are uniquely related to the degree to which the dominant, development-specific fast spindle type within an individual shares characteristics with adult-like fast sleep spindles.
source: In sum, our results suggest that developmental age differences in the manifestation of SO-spindle coupling are uniquely related to the degree to which the dominant, development-specific fast spindle type within an individual, that is, the sleep spindles that can be identified as peaks in the power spectrum (Aru et al., 2015; see Figure 1A), shares characteristics with adult-like fast sleep spindles.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined results from the maturity analyses.

claim: The temporally precise synchronization of sleep spindles during the up peak of SOs might not be an inherent feature of the thalamocortical system.
source: Overall, our findings suggest that the temporally precise synchronization of sleep spindles during the up peak of SOs might not be an inherent feature of the thalamocortical system.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the developmental findings showing that coupling precision develops over time.

claim: SO-spindle coupling patterns differ systematically across the lifespan.
source: Rather, SO-spindle coupling patterns differ systematically across the lifespan (Hahn et al., 2020; Helfrich et al., 2018; Joechner et al., 2021; Muehlroth et al., 2019), likely depending on age-specific anatomical and electrophysiological properties of the thalamocortical network.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and the current findings.

claim: Age-related dispersion and imprecision of frontal SO-spindle coupling in older adults were related to atrophy in the prefrontal cortex and the thalamus.
source: Previous research in older adults suggested that age-related dispersion and imprecision of frontal SO-spindle coupling were related to atrophy in the prefrontal cortex and the thalamus—brain sites critically involved in the generation of mature SOs and spindles, respectively (Helfrich et al., 2018; Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in older adults.

claim: The development of the well-known coupling of sleep spindles to SO up peaks is uniquely linked to the emergence of an increasing number of spindles in the canonical fast sleep spindle frequency range.
source: While these studies indirectly hypothesized that age-related changes in fast sleep spindle and SO features may contribute to alterations in the SO-spindle coupling pattern, we provide direct evidence that the development of the well-known coupling of sleep spindles to SO up peaks is uniquely linked to the emergence of an increasing number of spindles in the canonical fast sleep spindle frequency range.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding based on the data analyses.

claim: The duration of hyperpolarization and the resulting length of hyperpolarization-rebound sequences in thalamocortical cells particularly account for slower and faster spindle frequencies.
source: For one, the duration of hyperpolarization and the resulting length of hyperpolarization-rebound sequences in thalamocortical cells has been reported to particularly account for slower and faster spindle frequencies (Steriade, 2003; Steriade and Llinás, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Steriade, 2003 and Steriade and Llinás, 1988.

claim: Decreasing hyperpolarization in thalamocortical, and potentially reticular thalamic and cortical, cells may underly the global increase in the frequency of predominant sleep spindles across child and adolescent development.
source: Hence, decreasing hyperpolarization in thalamocortical, and potentially reticular thalamic and cortical, cells may underly the global increase in the frequency of predominant sleep spindles across child and adolescent development (Campbell and Feinberg, 2016; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known mechanisms and developmental observations, supported by citations.

claim: Both thalamic nuclei and thalamocortical connectivity are refined across development.
source: Further, both thalamic nuclei and thalamocortical connectivity are refined across development (Steiner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steiner et al., 2020.

claim: Studies indicate increased white matter and functional connectivity of thalamocortical tracts with older age—specifically with frontal, motor, and somatosensory cortical areas.
source: This applies to structural and functional changes with studies indicating increased white matter and functional connectivity of thalamocortical tracts with older age—specifically with frontal, motor, and somatosensory cortical areas (Avery et al., 2022; Fair et al., 2010; Steiner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Inter-individual differences in magnetic resonance imaging indicators of white matter properties were linked to the expression of spindle power and frequency.
source: Previously, inter-individual differences in magnetic resonance imaging indicators of white matter properties, supposed to index myelin-dependent efficiency in signal transmission (Chanraud et al., 2010), were linked to the expression of spindle power and frequency (Mander et al., 2017; Piantoni et al., 2013b; Sanchez et al., 2020; Vien et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Increased white matter integrity of certain thalamocortical projections may support the increase in sleep spindle frequency and higher numbers of fast sleep spindles with older age during development.
source: Therefore, increased white matter integrity of certain thalamocortical projections may support the increase in sleep spindle frequency and higher numbers of fast sleep spindles with older age during development.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the cited literature and the current findings.

claim: Primarily canonical fast sleep spindles coalesce with the up peak of SOs, while slow sleep spindles are synchronized more towards the down peak.
source: Importantly, accumulating findings support the conjecture that primarily canonical fast sleep spindles coalesce with the up peak of SOs, while slow sleep spindles are synchronized more towards the down peak (Bastian et al., 2022; Kurz et al., 2021; Mölle et al., 2011; Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Corticothalamic input is one of the most potent mechanisms inducing spindles.
source: While sleep spindles can be solely initiated in intra-thalamic circuits and thus could co-occur with SOs merely by chance, corticothalamic input is one of the most potent mechanisms inducing spindles (Bonjean et al., 2011; Contreras and Steriade, 1995; Helfrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The synchronous firing of cortical cells during the depolarizing SO up state can excite thalamic sleep spindle generation while the joint neuronal hyperpolarization during the down state terminates and inhibits spindles.
source: The connectivity between the cortex and the thalamus is supposed to explain the formation of SO-spindle modulation in a way that the synchronous firing of cortical cells during the depolarizing SO up state can excite thalamic sleep spindle generation while the joint neuronal hyperpolarization during the down state terminates and inhibits spindles (Contreras and Steriade, 1995; Steriade, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Enhanced SO-spindle coupling may index the development of thalamocortical pathways that give rise to sleep spindles at faster frequencies.
source: Hence, it is conceivable that enhanced SO-spindle coupling not only indexes the development of thalamocortical pathways (that may give rise to sleep spindles at faster frequencies) but also changes in corticothalamic connectivity allowing for increasingly efficient cortical control over spindle generation—specifically of canonical fast spindles (Contreras and Steriade, 1995).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known mechanisms and the current findings.

claim: Enhanced SO-spindle coupling may index changes in corticothalamic connectivity allowing for increasingly efficient cortical control over spindle generation—specifically of canonical fast spindles.
source: Hence, it is conceivable that enhanced SO-spindle coupling not only indexes the development of thalamocortical pathways (that may give rise to sleep spindles at faster frequencies) but also changes in corticothalamic connectivity allowing for increasingly efficient cortical control over spindle generation—specifically of canonical fast spindles (Contreras and Steriade, 1995).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known mechanisms and the current findings.

claim: A higher SO amplitude was associated with coupling strength.
source: For instance, a higher SO amplitude was associated with coupling strength (Kurz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kurz et al., 2021.

claim: In older adults, a diminished directional influence of SOs was related to imprecise SO-spindle coupling.
source: Further, in older adults, a diminished directional influence of SOs was related to imprecise SO-spindle coupling (Helfrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Helfrich et al., 2018.

claim: The precisely timed synchronization of sleep spindles during SO up peaks is in particular discussed as important for memory consolidation.
source: On a functional level, the precisely timed synchronization of sleep spindles during SO up peaks is in particular discussed as important for memory consolidation (Maingret et al., 2016; Niknazar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Developmental differences in SO-spindle coupling from late childhood to adolescence have been linked to developmental enhancements in memory consolidation.
source: In line with this, developmental differences in SO-spindle coupling from late childhood to adolescence have been linked to developmental enhancements in memory consolidation (García-Pérez et al., 2022; Hahn et al., 2020), implying less functional consolidation with less pronounced SO-spindle coupling (Helfrich et al., 2018; Muehlroth et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Already children can show extraordinary levels of sleep-associated memory consolidation.
source: Yet, already children can show extraordinary levels of sleep-associated memory consolidation (e.g., Peiffer et al., 2020; Urbain et al., 2016; Wilhelm et al., 2013), raising the question of which features during sleep might support such high levels of memory consolidation at young age.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In young children the development-specifically manifested SO-spindle coupling pattern was found to not yet be associated with memory consolidation while sleep spindles and SOs individually were.
source: Interestingly, in young children the development-specifically manifested SO-spindle coupling pattern was found to not yet be associated with memory consolidation while sleep spindles and SOs individually were (Joechner et al., 2021), implying that alternative features during sleep might compensate for less pronounced SO-spindle coupling (Wilhelm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Joechner et al., 2021.

claim: The ability to generate adult-like, canonical fast spindles determines coupling strength and precision across child and adolescent development.
source: While SOs provide optimal time windows for sleep spindles to arise, it is the ability to generate adult-like, canonical fast spindles that determines coupling strength and precision across child and adolescent development.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the main findings.

claim: The maturation of specific thalamocortical circuits is the cornerstone of adult-like SO-spindle coupling patterns.
source: Given the evidence for its generating role, our results implicate the maturation of specific thalamocortical circuits as the cornerstone of adult-like SO-spindle coupling patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the findings and known mechanisms.
